claims.claim: In 1517, Martin Luther, a monk and professor at the University of Wittenberg, wrote the Ninety-five Theses objecting to the sale of indulgences; by tradition he posted them on 31 October 1517.

Indulgences were understood in Catholic teaching as reducing or cancelling the temporal punishment (time in purgatory) a soul faced; by the sixteenth century some were sold, which reformers criticized.

Luther taught that faith alone is sufficient for salvation (sola fide) and that scripture alone should be the source of Christian belief and practice (sola scriptura). These are described as his theological positions in a dispute the Catholic Church rejected.
The printing press with movable type, developed in Europe around 1440 during the Renaissance, aided the rapid spread of Luther's message across Germany within about a year.
John Calvin, based in Geneva, taught the doctrine of predestination (that God had predetermined which souls would be saved) and published his Institutes of the Christian Religion in 1536.

In 1534, the English Parliament passed the Act of Supremacy, establishing the Church of England with the English monarch (Henry VIII) as its head, independent of the pope; this break began largely as a political and dynastic dispute.

The Council of Trent met in three sessions from 1545 to 1563 and reaffirmed that salvation requires both faith and good works and that scripture and church tradition are both authoritative; it forbade the sale of indulgences without abolishing indulgences, and enacted reforms.

The Reformation permanently divided Western Christianity; the Peace of Augsburg (1555) applied cuius regio, eius religio, and religious and political conflict contributed to the Thirty Years' War (1618-1648), ended by the Peace of Westphalia in 1648.

The Reformation's emphasis on vernacular scripture encouraged literacy and printing, and its long-term effects included strengthening state authority over churches and shaping later political thought.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The traditional story that Luther nailed the Ninety-five Theses to the Wittenberg castle church door on 31 October 1517 is well established but debated by some historians as to its literal accuracy.
positions: World History Encyclopedia gives the date 31 October 1517 for the posting.
OpenStax states the Theses were written and distributed in 1517 without asserting the door-posting as a certain physical event.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson dates the Theses to 1517 and frames the 31 October posting with 'according to tradition,' which both sources support without overstating a contested detail.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the Reformation was primarily religious or primarily political/economic.
positions: Doctrinal reading: it centered on theology (faith, scripture, salvation).
Structural reading: rulers' resentment of Church wealth and power and the printing revolution were decisive.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents multiple, combined causation (religious grievances plus political, economic, and technological factors) rather than choosing one.

sourceRecords.notes: Authoritative OER survey. Facts used; wording written originally.

sourceRecords.title: Council of Trent
sourceRecords.notes: Peer-reviewed encyclopedia entry. Supports the Council of Trent dates (1545-1563, three sessions, 25 meetings), its reaffirmation that one is saved by faith and the good works faith inspires (rejecting faith alone), its treatment of scripture and tradition, its reform of indulgences (no longer sold), and its role as the blueprint of the Catholic Counter-Reformation. Reference-only; no wording reproduced.
